title: The Four Weepings of the Rational: Sorrow at the Proprium and Sorrow at the End
reading:
As the Lord goes forth into the soul as the Divine Human, the rational accommodates itself downward through degrees, and in each degree it is clothed in an outer truth fitted to that level. These outer truths weep three times as the rational descends, and then they fall silent. There is also a fourth weeping, which comes at the end; that one too will be quieted, and after it is over the rational will never weep again.

The first weeping is the moment when the rational, going forth, sees the proprium for what it is — sees self-love stretched out at a distance against it, the contradiction it must enter. In that moment the rational knows everything that will come upon it: what will rise up against it, what it will have to bear through the natural mind that it is about to put on. Yet under the necessity by which the vessel must form, it goes in toward what it has seen. It weeps because it sees, and it goes in because it must; and after the three weepings of descent are complete, it grows still.

The fourth weeping is different. It belongs to the consummation, to the chosen moment when the final gathering takes place and all that is the Lord's is brought up into the regenerated whole. In that moment the rational weeps for the souls that have prepared themselves for falsity — souls that loved the darkness, set it continually before themselves hour by hour, and shaped their works toward it. Such souls, by the necessity of what they have desired, are bound to what they loved; they are separated off from the final gathering and cut away from the unity that the regenerated rational has become. They remain behind in their affliction forever, and from this hour onward no rest reaches them.

This is why the fourth weeping is greater than the first three. The earlier weepings were the sorrow of going down into the contest under necessity, knowing the proprium that had to be entered. The fourth is the sorrow of seeing those who, given the contest, gave themselves to what could not be raised — souls cut off from rest because no rest is possible for what has bound itself wholly to self-love. Even the structural boundaries of the rational, the firmaments that hold the degrees apart so that influx may be received, share in this grieving: they too weep over those who shall be cut off from rest, with a lamentation deeper than the three weepings of descent. It is not the weeping of going forth; it is the weeping of seeing some who will not return.
